hypothesis: Disease was caused by "miasma" -- poisonous vapors from rotting organic matter and foul air.
whyPlausible: Outbreaks of cholera, plague, and other diseases correlated with foul-smelling, unsanitary environments, and cleaning up filth often reduced illness.
contradicting: John Snow's 1854 investigation of a London cholera outbreak traced cases to a single contaminated water pump, not air quality; Koch and Pasteur later identified specific microbial agents for specific diseases.
whatChanged: The rise of germ theory in the late 19th century, backed by Koch's postulates, replaced miasma theory with the understanding that specific microorganisms cause specific diseases.

hypothesis: Living organisms, including microbes, could arise spontaneously from non-living matter under the right conditions.
whyPlausible: Meat left out seemed to spontaneously produce maggots, and broth left standing appeared to spontaneously grow microbial life.
contradicting: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiments (1859-1861) showed sterilized broth stayed lifeless unless exposed to airborne particles carrying microbes.
whatChanged: Pasteur's controlled experiments and the Alhumbert Prize verdict of 1862 effectively ended serious scientific support for spontaneous generation.

hypothesis: Peptic ulcers were caused purely by stress and excess stomach acid, unrelated to any infection.
whyPlausible: Stress and acid clearly worsened ulcer symptoms, and no bacterium was believed able to survive the stomach's acidic environment.
contradicting: Marshall and Warren's identification of Helicobacter pylori and Marshall's 1984 self-experiment showed a bacterium could colonize the stomach and cause gastritis.
whatChanged: Clinical trials confirmed antibiotics cured most ulcers linked to H. pylori infection, shifting medical consensus by the 1990s.

hypothesis: Because proteins are chemically more complex and varied than DNA, many scientists assumed proteins, not DNA, carried hereditary information.
whyPlausible: DNA was known to be made of only four repeating nucleotide building blocks, which seemed too simple to encode the complexity of heredity.
contradicting: The Avery-MacLeod-McCarty experiment (1944) and the Hershey-Chase experiment (1952) both showed DNA, not protein, transmits genetic information.
whatChanged: Direct experimental evidence, followed by Watson and Crick's 1953 double-helix model showing how DNA could encode information, ended the protein hypothesis.

hypothesis: Extremophile microorganisms later called archaea were assumed to simply be unusual types of bacteria adapted to harsh environments.
whyPlausible: Archaea share a similar cell size and lack of a nucleus with bacteria, and were not visibly distinct under standard microscopy.
contradicting: Carl Woese's 1977 comparative 16S rRNA analysis revealed archaea were genetically as distinct from bacteria as bacteria are from eukaryotes.
whatChanged: Molecular sequencing evidence led to the establishment of the three-domain system of life, separating Archaea from Bacteria.

hypothesis: Early researchers debated whether the filterable agent causing diseases like tobacco mosaic disease was a chemical toxin rather than a living organism.
whyPlausible: The agent passed through filters that trapped all known bacteria and could not be seen under contemporary microscopes, resembling a chemical rather than a cell.
contradicting: Later research showed the agent could replicate only inside living host cells and had a genome, distinguishing it from any non-living chemical poison.
whatChanged: Advances including the invention of the electron microscope in the 1930s allowed direct visualization of virus particles, confirming they were biological entities with defined structure, not simple chemicals.
